extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and writers seeking guidance on poetic composition and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing poetry and for conducting literary criticism: how critics should judge, what poets should follow, and what constitutes good taste, learning, and conduct in literary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your own reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure yourself and your own reach to know / How far your genius taste and learning go. / Launch not beyond your depth, but be discreet / And mark that point where sense and dullness meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess honestly your own talents, taste, and learning before attempting work or passing judgment. Do not attempt subjects beyond your competence; recognize limits where sound sense ends and folly begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: First follow nature
rubrics_metrics.description: First follow nature and your judgment frame / By her just standard, which is still the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat nature (human nature, truth, and the appearances of life) as the primary standard for poetic creation and critical judgment. Rules should derive from and conform to nature's 'just standard.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are methodized nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Those rules, of old discovered, not devised, / Are nature still, but nature methodized;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that classical precepts are codifications of natural principles. Study them as organized forms of natural artistic law rather than arbitrary inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the ancients and their context
rubrics_metrics.description: Know well each ancient's proper character, / His fable subject scope in every page, / Religion, country, genius of his age
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and meditate on canonical authors (Homer, Horace, Longinus, Quintilian, etc.). Learn each author's historical, cultural, and stylistic context before applying or criticizing their rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow license sparingly and with precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: If, where the rules not far enough extend... That license is a rule. ... But though the ancients thus their rules invade... Moderns beware! or if you must offend / Against the precept, ne'er transgress its end, / Let it be seldom, and compelled by need, / And have, at least, their precedent to plead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative departures from rules (licenses) can be justified when they serve the work's intent, are rare, and have precedent among recognized masters; do not transgress rules merely for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false learning and pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Some dryly plain, without invention's aid, / Write dull receipts how poems may be made / These leave the sense their learning to display, / And those explain the meaning quite away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute display of erudition for genuine sense or invention. Learning should serve the poetry's meaning, not obscure or replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid half-learned affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those half-learned witlings, numerous in our isle, / As half-formed insects on the banks of Nile / Unfinished things one knows not what to call
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the 'half-learned' critic or writer who displays incomplete knowledge and thereby produces confused or affected work; strive for thorough understanding rather than superficial display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know an author's aims before criticizing
rubrics_metrics.description: In every work regard the writer's end, / Since none can compass more than they intend;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem against the aims and intentions of its author. If means are appropriate and conduct true to intent, minor faults should not lead to harsh condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a work with the author's spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect judge will read each work of wit / With the same spirit that its author writ
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathetic reading—trying to apprehend the work as the author conceived it—is essential to fair criticism. Avoid reading solely from external standards detached from the work's spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the whole; avoid nitpicking parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey the whole nor seek slight faults to find / Where nature moves and rapture warms the mind, / Nor lose for that malignant dull delight / The generous pleasure to be charmed with wit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow the search for minor defects to override appreciation of a work's overall effect and vitality. Critics should weigh global achievement over trivial imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit is nature dressed to advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: True wit is nature to advantage dressed; / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for expression that clarifies and elevates natural thought; avoid ornate embellishment that conceals absence of real insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style and sound to subject and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis not enough no harshness gives offense, / The sound must seem an echo to the sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form (diction, rhythm, sound) should reflect and amplify content and emotion. Gentle subjects require soft numbers; violent subjects require forceful lines (examples: Ajax vs. Camilla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical variation should follow the passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Hear how Timotheus' varied lays surprise, / And bid alternate passions fall and rise!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ variation in cadence and musicality to produce and sustain emotional changes in the poem—use rhythmic shifts to echo changes in feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes in judgment and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extremes, and shun the fault of such, / Who still are pleased too little or too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer a middle course between slavish admiration and perpetual detraction; both excesses reflect poor judgment and pride or ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate technical regularity with excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: In wit, as nature, what affects our hearts / Is not the exactness of peculiar parts... 'Tis not a lip, or eye, we beauty call, / But the joint force and full result of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfectly regular but lifeless piece may be technically correct yet uninspiring; value organic unity and overall impact over mechanical perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging by metric smoothness alone
rubrics_metrics.description: But most by numbers judge a poet's song / And smooth or rough, with them is right or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce poetic quality to matching syllable counts or predictable rhymes; avoid critics who favor mere tunefulness over sense and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be the first to try the new nor the last to abandon the old
rubrics_metrics.description: Be not the first by whom the new are tried, / Nor yet the last to lay the old aside
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise prudence with novelty: neither rush headlong into untested fashions nor cling stubbornly to outdated modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conceit and ornament that mask lack of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets, like painters, thus, unskilled to trace / The naked nature and the living grace, / With gold and jewels cover every part, / And hide with ornaments their want of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamentation should not be used to conceal poverty of thought or structure; simplicity and fidelity to nature are marks of true artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: False eloquence, like the prismatic glass... Its gaudy colors spreads on every place, / The face of nature we no more survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamboyant language that distorts or obscures natural meaning should be avoided; clarity that improves thought is preferable to mere verbal splendor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility: distrust pride; consult friends and foes
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust not yourself, but your defects to know, / Make use of every friend--and every foe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride blinds judgment; seek corrective feedback widely (including from rivals) to identify defects in your work or criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire deep learning; shallow knowledge misleads
rubrics_metrics.description: A little learning is a dangerous thing / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial acquaintance with learning intoxicates and misleads; pursue serious study if you will judge or practice in the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share counsel courteously; teach tactfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Men must be taught as if you taught them not. / Without good breeding truth is disapproved; / That only makes superior sense beloved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver correction and instruction with tact and good manners so that truth is accepted rather than rejected; civility enhances persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give advice freely but responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be niggards of advice on no pretense; / For the worst avarice is that of sense / With mean complacence, ne'er betray your trust, / Nor be so civil as to prove unjust
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hoard knowledge out of pride, but don't give advice in a way that betrays trust or flatters unjustly; be generous yet honest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict censure; silence can be charitable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis best sometimes your censure to restrain, / And charitably let the dull be vain / Your silence there is better than your spite
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes withholding harsh criticism is kinder and more useful—dull writers will often continue without being harmed by silence, whereas spite only perpetuates ill effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flattery and sycophancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave dangerous truths to unsuccessful satires, / And flattery to fulsome dedicators / Whom, when they praise, the world believes no more, / Than when they promise to give scribbling o'er.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist flattering influential patrons and avoid compromising praise for gain. Honest appraisal should not be traded for favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge works, not names or reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judge of authors names not works, and then / Nor praise nor blame the writing, but the men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let an author's fame or social status determine your judgment; evaluate the actual work on its merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid herd opinion and fickleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ne'er advance a judgment of their own, / But catch the spreading notion of the town, / They reason and conclude by precedent, / And own stale nonsense which they ne'er invent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent judgment is required; avoid simply echoing public opinion or changing views with the crowd for fashion's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the ideal critic
rubrics_metrics.description: Unbiased, or by favor, or in spite, / Not dully prepossessed, nor blindly right; / Though learned, well-bred, and though well bred, sincere, / Modestly bold, and humanly severe, / Who to a friend his faults can freely show, / And gladly praise the merit of a foe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exemplary critic is learned but modest, unbiased, sincere, courageous in reproof, generous in praise, humane yet exacting—able to correct friends and praise enemies honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should be the muse's handmaid
rubrics_metrics.description: Then criticism the muse's handmaid proved, / To dress her charms, and make her more beloved:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The function of criticism is to serve and refine the art, to illuminate and improve poetry rather than to destroy or merely police it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject envy and malicious criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride, malice, folly against Dryden rose... Envy will merit, as its shade, pursue, / But like a shadow, proves the substance true:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and discard criticism motivated by envy, pride, or malice. True merit withstands such attacks; critics should aim to be just rather than vindictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn obscenity regardless of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: No pardon vile obscenity should find, / Though wit and art conspire to move your mind;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenity and corrupting content should not be excused on the grounds of cleverness or artistry—moral considerations matter in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scandalous over-scrutiny that misattributes vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet shun their fault, who, scandalously nice, / Will needs mistake an author into vice; / All seems infected that the infected spy, / As all looks yellow to the jaundiced eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While condemning vice is right, do not be so suspicious that you falsely impute vice where none exists; a jaundiced critic sees faults everywhere.
